\chapter{Why Se? --- Gelo, and a Collision}
\label{ch:etymon-gelo}
\hlchaptermodality{100}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say why le becomes se, and that this se is not the reflexive one.}

Complete ES-C47-por-que-se: name the Old Spanish form, and say whether the se of se lo digo is the se of se llama.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[gelo to se lo]{Why se? — and why it is not the se you know}

\label{lesson:ES-C47-por-que-se}



\begin{quote}
You have known a word \emph{se} since almost the beginning: \emph{se llama}, \textquotedblleft{}he calls \textbf{himself}.\textquotedblright{} Now you have met a second \emph{se}, in \emph{se lo digo}. The obvious conclusion is that they are the same word doing a second job.

They are not. They are two different words that arrived at the same spelling, and knowing that removes a confusion most learners carry for years.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Old Spanish did not say \emph{se lo}. It said \textbf{gelo}.

That came from the two Latin pronouns you already know, run together and worn down: \emph{illī} (the dative, giving \emph{le}) plus \emph{illum} (the accusative, giving \emph{lo}) $\to$ \textbf{gelo}. One squeezed word for \textquotedblleft{}to-him it.\textquotedblright{}

So the medieval sentence was \emph{gelo digo}, and it was regular. There was no substitution and no rule to learn.

Then two things happened:

1. \textbf{The word split back into two} — \emph{gelo} was re-analysed as \emph{ge} + \emph{lo}, matching the two-pronoun pattern everywhere else in the language. 2. \textbf{The sound \emph{ge} drifted} until it was pronounced exactly like \emph{se} — and once two words sound identical, spelling follows.

By the sixteenth century \emph{ge lo} had become \emph{se lo}, and the trail was cold.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
This matters for a practical reason, not a historical one.

The reflexive \emph{se} in \emph{se llama} means \textbf{himself}. If the \emph{se} in \emph{se lo digo} were that word, the sentence would have to mean something reflexive — and learners who assume it do spend years trying to make \textquotedblleft{}he tells it to himself\textquotedblright{} fit sentences where it plainly does not.

It does not fit because it is not that word. One \emph{se} is Latin \emph{sē}, \textquotedblleft{}himself\textquotedblright{}; the other is \emph{illī}, \textquotedblleft{}to him.\textquotedblright{} Unrelated, and collided by accident of sound.

Two words wearing one shape is something this language does often — \emph{ser} is built from two Latin verbs, \emph{ir} borrows its present from a third. Here it happens to two of the smallest words in Spanish, which is where it is hardest to notice.
\end{culture}

\end{itemize}
